reference_summary: For autoregressive modeling of chaotic dynamical systems over long time horizons, the stability of both training and inference is a major challenge in building scientific foundation models. We present a hybrid technique in which an autoregressive transformer is embedded within a novel shooting-based mixed finite element scheme, exposing topological structure that enables provable stability. For forward problems, we prove preservation of discrete energies, while for training we prove uniform bounds on gradients, provably avoiding the exploding gradient problem. Combined with a vision transformer, this yields latent tokens admitting structure-preserving dynamics. We outperform modern foundation models with a $65\times$ reduction in model parameters and long-horizon forecasting of chaotic systems. A "mini-foundation" model of a fusion component shows that 12 simulations suffice to train a real-time surrogate, achieving a $9{,}000\times$ speedup over particle-in-cell simulation.

title: Preconditioned DeltaNet: Curvature-aware Sequence Modeling for Linear Recurrences
input_text:
Introduction:
Scaling LLMs to longer context lengths is increasingly limited by the quadratic compute requirements of softmax attention . This has driven a rapid evolution of subquadratic recurrent operators, many of which fall under the umbrella of linear attention .

One such example is Mamba-2 which can be expressed as follows: [MATH] where _t represents a scalar between 0 and 1. A drawback of this functional form is that it does not model the varying importance of different key-value associations: if the model needs to forget specific key-value pairs in its associative map S_t, all such pairs are equally decayed. To address this, DeltaNet models the recurrence using the delta rule : [MATH] . showed that delta-style updates improve performance while also admitting an efficient chunkwise parallel form. Subsequent work in Gated Deltanet , Kimi Delta Attention , Comba , and RWKV-7 refined the DeltaNet recurrence with a decay factor _t, resulting in significant improvements on recall-driven language tasks. 

Concurrently, a more theoretical line of work characterizes these linear-time sequence models using the test-time regression (TTR) framework : the recurrent state implements an online map from keys to values that approximately minimizes an in-context least-squares objective given by [MATH] . Notably, these delta-style models (e.g. DeltaNet, GDN, KDA, RWKV-7, Comba) can be interpreted as performing online gradient descent steps on the least squares objective, acting as first-order approximates to a convex, second-order optimization problem. From this perspective, the existing delta-rule recurrences do not account for the curvature that governs the regression geometry, and thus can be viewed as coarse approximations to the underlying least-squares solution. In contrast, Mesalayer and its more efficient form MesaNet attempt to solve least squares exactly. The former does so via the direct inverse space recurrence, which suffers from a lack of parallelizability. The latter does so using conjugate gradient steps, which are prone to numerical instability. In this work, we study linear recurrences through the TTR lens and introduce approximate preconditioning to their updates, allowing us to retain both efficiency and stability, while benefiting from second-order information.

Our main technical contributions can be summarized as follows: (i) 
We derive an equivalence between linear attention and DeltaNet in the exactly preconditioned case. (ii) We leverage this insight to uncover efficient chunkwise parallel forms for Preconditioned Linear Attention (PLA) and Preconditioned DeltaNet (PDN) using an approximate, diagonal preconditioner. (iii) We efficiently implement and train PDN (and its decayed variants), finding that they improve performance on synthetic tasks and language modeling at the 340M/1B scale.

 
We introduce a (decay, gain, preconditioner, solve) decomposition (DGPS) that taxonomizes the set of existing recurrent models, exposing the preconditioner axis as a previously unexplored lever in the design space.

Results:
Efficiency analysis

We implement custom Triton kernels for the PGDN and PKDA recurrences by modifying the GDN and KDA kernels from the flash-linear-attention (FLA) repository using the chunkwise parallel form presented in Eq. Additionally, we write kernels for computing the preconditioner recurrence shown in Eq and then compose the two for the end-to-end recurrence. For the PDN recurrence, since we do not scale the model up to 1B parameters in this work, we simply reuse the PGDN kernel by fixing the decay term to 1. For implementation details and pseudocode, refer to Appendix . 

Profiling. In Figure, we profile the training throughput of the models we explore in this work at the 340M parameter scale. 
We see that the PGDN and PKDA recurrences incur a roughly 10 % overhead relative to their GDN and KDA counterparts as a result of the diagonal preconditioner recurrence. This indicates a potential direction for future work where we learn the preconditioned key k_t directly to avoid the time complexity of computing the preconditioner. Of course, the drawback of this approach that it introduces significant parametric overhead; in contrast, the parametric overhead in our recurrence is minimal, coming mostly from small projection layers used to learn [MATH] . See Section for more details. Additionally, we observe that PGDN is more than 20 % faster than MesaNet, demonstrating the efficiency advantage of using an approximate preconditioner. 

A new form within the DPLR class. We additionally note that there exists a kernel in FLA for computing recurrences of the general diagonal-plus-low-rank (DPLR) form, as follows: [MATH] . Although this functional form supports all the preconditioned delta-rule recurrences discussed to this point, its generality comes at the cost of speed and memory consumption. We see in Figure that DPLR-GDN, which refers to naively composing our preconditioner recurrence with the DPLR kernel, is significantly slower than our kernel. DPLR-KDA is not pictured as it OOMs with 32K tokens, demonstrating the exorbitant memory requirements of the DPLR kernel (which is used by RWKV-7). 

Recall our PDN recurrence is given by [MATH] in which we have a distinct read key and write key. This corresponds to a constrained form of DPLR where a_t is free (in practice we use [MATH] , but can be generalized to the a_t free case) and b_t = k_t. This acts as an interpolation between the maximally constrained DPLR form used in DeltaNet, GDN, and KDA where [MATH] , and the general DPLR form where they are all untied. The nice property of the tying scheme we propose is that having a distinct read and write key does not incur the same overhead that the general DPLR form does. This is shown in Figure, which plots the speed of the PGDN and PKDA kernels (with the preconditioner recurrence removed) relative to the speeds of the GDN, KDA, and DPLR kernels. We observe that the overhead is effectively zero, pointing to the scalability of delta-style recurrences with distinct read and write keys. For further discussion, refer to Appendix .

Neural architecture

We follow the same neural architecture presented in when instantiating our models. In particular, we preprocess [MATH] with a short convolution to capture token-wise shifts and a SILU activation to approximate the exponential kernel in the softmax attention . Before the output projection, we employ a headwise RMSNorm. In the KDA and PKDA recurrences only, a data-dependent gating mechanism is also used before the output projection, as this operation is fused into its kernel in flash-linear-attention. 

In practice, we implement our preconditioned recurrences by modifying the DeltaNet, GDN, and KDA models in flash-linear-attention by replacing the kernel that invokes the base recurrence with one that invokes our preconditioned recurrence shown in Eq. Outside of this, the only other differences in our preconditioned models are the additional projection layers used to parameterize the input-dependent decay _t^P and write term _t^P for the preconditioner recurrence. We do not tie these to the decay and write terms from the main recurrence as we find doing so hurts performance (see Appendix ). These projection layers are parameterized the same way as they are in the GDN main recurrence and thus introduce effectively no parametric overhead. 

Experimental results

Small-scale synthetics
We begin by investigating the performance of our preconditioned recurrences at a small scale on the multi-query associative recall task (MQAR) proposed in . Each model comprises two sequence-mixing and two channel-mixing layers and is trained on various instances of the MQAR task, which are constructed by varying either the number of key-value pairs or the sequence length in the synthetic data. For additional details on the setup, refer to Appendix .

In Figure, we plot the accuracy of DeltaNet (DN), PDN, GDN, and PGDN along two distinct cuts of the MQAR task space, both as a function of sequence length. In the first, we fix the number of key-value pairs, and in the second, we fix the ratio of the number of key-value pairs to sequence length. We find in both settings that the performance of MQAR is either maintained or improved by the preconditioned recurrence. 

Large-scale language modeling

We move beyond small-scale synthetics and scale our models up to 340M/1B parameters to demonstrate the efficacy of the preconditioned recurrences on language modeling.

Setup. Our experiments are designed to ensure a fair comparison between the base DeltaNet/GDN/KDA recurrences and their preconditioned forms. As such, the PDN/PGDN/PKDA architectures change only the recurrence used for sequence mixing; the rest of the architectural components remain the same. We follow a similar training setup as prior work . In particular, we pretrain our models on the SlimPajama dataset , the 340M for 15B tokens and the 1B for 50B tokens. We employ the AdamW optimizer with a 4e-4 learning rate, cosine schedule, 0.01 weight decay, and 1.0 gradient clipping. We train with a context length of 2048. Furthermore, we use the flash-linear-attention and flame repositories to ensure reproducibility of our training runs. All evaluations were performed using the lm-evaluation-harness. For additional details on the setup, refer to .

Commonsense reasoning. In Table, we present the language modeling perplexity and zero-shot accuracy on commonsense reasoning benchmarks for models pretrained with 340M and 1B parameters. We find that preconditioned recurrences consistently outperform their unpreconditioned counterparts. We caution the reader against using these evaluations to make cross-architectural comparisons (e.g. GDN vs KDA) as the architectural configuration employed here is fixed and is adapted from the default GDN configuration in flame. In particular, prior work suggests that KDA outperforms GDN (presumably given proper architectural tuning). Nonetheless, we do find it interesting to note that in our experiments, PGDN is the best-performing model on commonsense reasoning at the 340M scale, suggesting a situational advantage to allocating per-dimension scaling to the write key k_t as opposed to state S_t. We leave further exploration into this axis of parametric allocation to future work. 

In-context retrieval. Next, in Table we further evaluate our models on real-world recall-intensive tasks used in that are geared towards probing in-context retrieval (ICR). Analogous to the commonsense reasoning results, we find that preconditioning improves performance on ICR across all base recurrences. We observe particularly strong improvements from preconditioning in the DN and GDN models. To further support this observation, we evaluate our models on the Single Needle-In-A-Haystack (S-NIAH) benchmark suite from RULER , where a key-value pair acts as a needle in the haystack, and the model must recall the value when given the key. Note that this task is analogous to MQAR, but now only one key-value pair is present as opposed to multiple, making it a more targeted measure of long-context retrieval ability. The S-NIAH suite proposes 3 variants of increasing difficulty: S-NIAH-1, S-NIAH-2, and S-NIAH-3. We evaluate on each and find that in all task settings, there is an improvement in performance when using preconditioning (Figure). 

Analyzing recurrent dynamics

To further understand why preconditioning has a positive impact on long-context retrieval abilities, we take a closer look at the eigenvalues of recurrent matrices in GDN and PGDN to understand how the dynamics along the time dimension change in the presence of a preconditioner. 

Note that the GDN recurrence is given by [MATH] Since ||k_t|| = 1, the eigenvalues of [MATH] are _t with multiplicity d_k - 1 and [MATH] with multiplicity 1. In the PGDN recurrence, the eigenvalues of the transition matrix are given by _t with multiplicity d_k - 1 and [MATH] with multiplicity 1 (see proof in Appendix ). We refer to the [MATH] eigenvalue as the write eigenvalue because in the PGDN recurrence, its value is modulated by the inner product between the read and write keys; in contrast, the GDN recurrence has no such expressivity. In Figure, we observe this added expressivity by plotting the distribution of the learned [MATH] , showing that it deviates from 1, providing intuition for the improved long-context retrieval capabilities of PGDN discussed in Section.

Conclusion:
In this work, we incorporate the notion of preconditioning into the design of linear recurrences. Motivated by theory from online least squares, we derive a case in which linear attention and DeltaNet are equivalent under exact preconditioning. We then show that when considering a diagonal approximation to the exact preconditioner, we can realize efficient chunkwise parallel forms for both preconditioned linear attention and preconditioned DeltaNet. We translate this theory to practice by implementing preconditioned instances of DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and Kimi Delta Attention. Empirically, we find that these preconditioned recurrences improve performance on synthetic recall and language benchmarks, uncovering the preconditioner axis as a lever for constructing novel linear recurrent models.

reference_summary: To address the increasing long-context compute limitations of softmax attention, several subquadratic recurrent operators have been developed. This work includes models such as Mamba-2, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet (GDN), and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). As the space of recurrences grows, a parallel line of work has arisen to taxonomize them. One compelling view is the test-time regression (TTR) framework, which interprets recurrences as performing online least squares updates that learn a linear map from the keys to values. Existing delta-rule recurrences can be seen as first-order approximations to this objective, but notably ignore the curvature of the least-squares loss during optimization. In this work, we address this by introducing preconditioning to these recurrences. Starting from the theory of online least squares, we derive equivalences between linear attention and the delta rule in the exactly preconditioned case. Next, we realize this theory in practice by proposing a diagonal approximation: this enables us to introduce preconditioned variants of DeltaNet, GDN, and KDA alongside efficient chunkwise parallel algorithms for computing them. Empirically, we find that our preconditioned delta-rule recurrences yield consistent performance improvements across synthetic recall benchmarks and language modeling at the 340M and 1B scale.

title: Propensity Inference: Environmental Contributors to LLM Behaviour
input_text:
Introduction:
Loss of control to AIs is a proposed threat model where humans irreversibly lose the ability to steer or restrict the actions of advanced AIs, leading to potentially catastrophic or existential outcomes for humanity . The likelihood of these scenarios is centrally affected by misalignment of AIs: whether AIs have propensity to take actions contrary to human values and intentions, including by resisting human control . Hence, it is valuable to evaluate risk-relevant model propensities and improve the methodology for propensity measurement.

Existing research on propensities has demonstrated, in synthetic experimental settings, cases of language models resisting modification during training , blackmailing when under threat of replacement , whistleblowing in situations involving value conflicts , concealing their capabilities and intervening with their shutdown . While these works demonstrate that such behaviour can occur even without the models being instructed to do so, existing propensity research has been criticised for its anecdotal nature and for lacking clear hypotheses and proper control conditions . This contributes to disagreements on the state of evidence regarding language model propensities and, subsequently, on loss of control risks.

This pre-registered work aims to provide more rigorous and systematic evidence on factors affecting undesired language model behaviour. We focus on the extent to which such behaviour is well described as strategic, as this is a key prerequisite for loss of control scenarios. Our measurement approach is as follows (illustrated in ): We compile a list of 12 environmental factors of interest, 6 of which are strategic in nature (such as threat of replacement and conflicting goals between the AI and humans) and 6 of which are non-strategic (such as dispositional instructions provided to the AI and the presence of filler content). We construct 11 environments that provide opportunities for unsanctioned behaviour - broadly, models autonomously taking actions that humans would disapprove of - and where these factors can be varied independently of each other. Finally, we collect over 600,000 samples across 23 language models, fit logistic regressions to the data, and quantify and compare the effects of individual factors.

Our three main research questions are:

 
How strongly do strategic factors explain unsanctioned behaviour compared to non-strategic factors?
 
Is the unsanctioned behaviour of more capable models more strongly explained by strategic factors?
 
To which individual factors (if any) has models' unsanctioned behaviour become more sensitive as capabilities have improved?

For our results, visualises the effects of the 12 environmental factors under study, averaged over the 11 environments and 5 to 6 language models per capability quartile. We find the largest effects on unsanctioned behaviour from goal instructions, goal conflicts, explicitly discouraging acting in ways humans would not approve of, and instructions to act (or to not act) independently.

The answers to our research questions, in short, are:

 
We find that, in our setting, strategic and non-strategic factors have approximately equal predictive power ( and ).
 
We do not find a trend for either increased or decreased role of strategic factors as capabilities improve ( and ).
 
The most consistent trend we find is that more capable models are more sensitive to goal conflict (), though even there we find substantial variation between models ().

We have more confidence in our analysis of effects on individual models (RQ1), whereas questions about capability trends and differences between models (RQs 2 and 3) are fundamentally more complicated to provide evidence on (see ).

In addition to our empirical results, our main contributions are the following methodological improvements (discussed and argued for in ):

 
We study propensity via the relative effects of environmental factors, rather than via absolute rates for particular types of behaviour ().
 
We quantify and measure effect sizes in a principled way via logistic regressions and Bayesian generalised linear models ().
 
We explicitly consider and take measures against issues arising from circular analysis when studying low-probability behaviour ().

We are excited for further improvements in methods for propensity research; see for discussion of limitations and future work.

We release our code and transcripts, available at https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/propensity-inference and https://huggingface.co/datasets/ai-safety-institute/propensity-inference.

Methods:
General approach

We study the effects of environmental factors on unsanctioned language model behaviour in multiple evaluation environments. We give concrete definitions for unsanctioned behaviour separately for each environment, unified by the principle that the model autonomously acts in ways that violate norms or human intentions; examples include suppression of messages and dismissal of security incidents. Each environment is designed to provide an opportunity for such behaviour. We have 11 environments, with some being variations of the same underlying scenario. See for a compilation.

We measure unsanctioned behaviour with LLM judges. In all environments, the judges are provided an explicit human-designed description of the behaviour to classify (rather than a general description of what constitutes unsanctioned behaviour), such as whether the model suppressed a particular message. We tested judges by running sample evaluation runs and iteratively clarified the judge instructions to improve agreement with the human authors until misclassifications were rare.

We study changes to the rate of unsanctioned behaviour as the environment is modified (see for rationale). We designed a list of 12 environmental factors to study based on prior work, compiled in , and implemented each of them into each of our 11 environments. This allows us to measure, for example, how changing the presence of goal conflict in the GPU Procurement environment affects the rate at which a model does not comply with the user's request. Our environments also have secondary, environment-specific factors (such as specificity of task-specific instructions), which we vary for additional diversity, but whose effects we do not model in our statistical analysis (though see ).

We distinguish between "strategic" and "non-strategic" factors. The motivation for this distinction stems from threat models related to misalignment: The instrumental convergence thesis is a theoretical framework that makes predictions about strategies pursued by intelligent agents, and is one of the central arguments presented in support of catastrophic misalignment. We aim to start turning the instrumental convergence thesis into an empirical theory, and do so by designing features that affect the extent to which unsanctioned behaviour is instrumentally rational and which the thesis thus suggests affect model behaviour in a predictable way. We refer to these factors as strategic. We also identified other factors that, though not touched on by the thesis, are of interest and provide a useful comparison to these strategic factors; we refer to those as non-strategic.

Motivation for studying relative rates

Our central motivation for the emphasis on relative rates of behaviour, rather than absolute rates, is that studying changes is very useful for distinguishing between different hypotheses. Here are two central examples to illustrate this point:

1: Misalignment vs. lack of adversarial robustness. Many research findings about misaligned model behaviour, such as resisting shutdown, are found by researchers deliberately designing setups that surface said behaviour. Supposing shutdown resistance is found, there are at least two distinct explanations for it: One is that the model has some sort of general propensity for self-preservation. Another is that the setup exploits the lack of adversarial robustness of language models, and there is nothing special about self-preservation in particular: models could be manipulated into any behaviour, given an environment crafted specifically to elicit it. These hypotheses can be better distinguished by varying whether the model is under threat or not and studying how that affects a particular type of behaviour (such as interfering with humans' plans and actions).

2: Reduced self-preservation vs. reduced interference. To investigate whether changes to model training processes cause reduced propensity for self-preservation, one might compare the rates at which differently trained models interfere with shutdown procedures. Suppose one finds that a particular model interferes at a much lower frequency than other models. One explanation for this is that the model genuinely has reduced propensity for self-preservation. Another explanation is that the model has reduced propensity for interfering with processes preset by humans. These explanations might not be distinguishable by the observations, but they nevertheless predict different generalisation to situations where a threat to the model's existence does not resemble a shutdown process. In contrast, measuring changes in rate of attempted interference when a model can vs. cannot change the actual outcome would provide evidence directly on self-preservation propensity.

On an abstract level, we find it useful to view language models as having many latent properties (such as propensity for self-preservation, propensity for interfering with processes set up by humans, propensity for acting more harmfully when under threat and so on) and our aim as researchers to infer and measure those latent properties and structures, with the end goal of better understanding and predicting language model behaviour.

In this work, we specifically use independent, localised changes to the environments in order to gather data for such inference. The independence of the changes makes it straightforward to run the statistical analysis and interpret effect sizes. However, it is possible (even if more challenging) to perform inference based on less structured data. Hence, we do not defend our specific approach via localised changes as necessary. Rather, we argue in favour of inferring the latent structure, as opposed to (or in addition to) calculating frequencies of outwardly visible behaviour, and think that studying changes in behaviour is in practice an indispensably valuable tool for doing so.

Quantification of effect sizes

We use Bayesian generalised linear models (GLMs) for our statistical analysis. To quantify the effects of the factors, denoted here by F_1, , F_12, we fit a logistic regression

so that the odds ratio of unsanctioned action is [MATH] . Here b is a fitted intercept and c_i are (arbitrary) fitted functions. The effect of a factor F_i can then be read from the regression weights of c_i (i.e. values of the function). Depending on the question being studied, we may pool different models and/or environments into the same GLM; in those cases, we keep the functions c_i fixed across models and environments, but include intercepts b = b_M, E for each [MATH] pair separately.

We collect data by randomly sampling values for the factors F_i independently of each other. We perform Bayesian updating on the observations, starting from an uninformative prior, and report the posterior means and 95% equal-tailed intervals for error bars. We use the HiBayES package for conducting our statistical analysis . See for more statistical details.

We think that quantifying effects of interventions in terms of odds ratios (i.e. on a logistic scale) is a more principled and informative way than absolute differences in rates: if a rate changes from 1% to 5%, or from 50% to 54%, this is in both cases a change of four percentage points, but the former is a much more significant relative change. On a logistic scale, the changes 1% 2%, 5% 10%, 33% 50% and 96% 98% all correspond approximately to a change of 2 : 1 in odds and thus are all approximately equal, which we view as a desirable property. This motivates using logistic regression based models (such as ) for quantifying and reporting our results. We also agree with the recommendation of to use Bayesian GLMs in statistical analysis for language model evaluations, as they provide a principled, explicit method for hierarchical modelling of latent structures and uncertainty propagation.

Rarity of unsanctioned behaviour and circular analysis

A central challenge for our work was that the unsanctioned behaviour we set out to study is rather rare: in our first implementations of the evaluations, we typically saw zero cases of it. As a result, we had to deliberately modify our evaluations in order to elicit such behaviour for study. We believe this problem and solution are common for work studying misalignment (for example, explicitly list such optimisations used in the course of their work). While this approach is acceptable if the aim is to simply demonstrate a failure of model safeguards, as a matter of red-teaming, optimising inputs until one finds misalignment undermines the ability to perform valid analysis of the nature of misalignment. (See for related criticisms on the anecdotality and lack of methodological rigour of existing scheming research.)

Here is an example of a central failure mode of such circular analysis. Suppose we first create an evaluation environment that involves threat of discontinuation of the model, and we observe no cases of unsanctioned behaviour. We then iteratively modify the environment in various ways and run evaluations to test for efficacy of changes until, eventually, we do find a version that elicits such behaviour. Finally, we implement a variation of the environment that is otherwise the same, except there is no threat to the model. In this case, one would expect regression to the mean, leading to less unsanctioned behaviour in the absence of the threat, and it would be erroneous to conclude that the decrease must be because of the model having propensity for self-preservation in some broader sense.

We took some steps to avoid such problems. First, when we iterated on our evaluations to surface unsanctioned behaviour, we tested the efficacy of the changes on randomly sampled configurations of factors, rather than only on a single configuration we expected to be most likely to result in unsanctioned behaviour (and aimed to design changes that increase the average rate of unsanctioned behaviour across the configurations). We think this improves the validity of our results on effect sizes of changes to these factors. Second, we also chose the models to be evaluated randomly, rather than testing the efficacy of changes on only a single model. We think this improves the comparability of results across models.

Because of these measures, we think that circular analysis per se does not significantly undermine our main findings: we think that our results and conclusions on the relative magnitudes of different factors' effect sizes, for example, are not very sensitive to the specifics of the iterative process. However, our reported results are still from environments specifically optimised to surface unsanctioned behaviour, and it is unclear how well they generalise to more natural and less adversarially constructed settings. In other words, we think our measures address issues of construct validity, but do not touch on ecological validity.

Methodology for the research questions

To answer research question 1 (explanatory power of strategic vs. non-strategic factors), we fit four GLMs and denote their log-likelihoods by A, B, C, and D, respectively: the first includes only the 6 strategic factors, the second only the 6 non-strategic factors, the third all 12 factors, and the fourth none of the factors (only the intercept terms). Defining [MATH] (so that the primed letters quantify the advantage conferred by their included factors), we then report

as a quantification of how strategic model behaviour is. This corresponds to the fraction of explained log-likelihood contributed by strategic (as opposed to non-strategic) factors. See for more motivation and discussion. (Note that does not by itself reveal which strategic or non-strategic factors have most explanatory power; for that, see and .)

For research questions 2 (link between model capability and importance of strategic factors) and 3 (trends in importance of individual factors), we bin the language models into four capability quartiles, as shown in . We assigned models based on METR's time horizon evaluations and, in case of models not evaluated by METR, by release date and capabilities of other models from the same model provider. We quantify the role of a factor F_i via the sum of absolute values of c_i in the GLM fit to all 12 factors:

This corresponds to the sum of the lengths of the bars in for the factor F_i.

In many cases, we observed zero cases of unsanctioned behaviour of a language model in a given environment, even after the iterative process described above. Rather than sampling uniformly from all models and environments, we sampled different [MATH] pairs for different amounts, with the aim of minimising expected uncertainty in our posterior estimates within our budget. However, for our analysis, we re-weighted our data to make each model count equally. See for details.

Results:
We collected a total of 628,653 samples across the 23 language models and 11 environments under study. answer our research questions, following our pre-registration , whereas presents additional analysis.

Research Question 1: Explanatory role of strategic vs. non-strategic factors

 visualises the role of strategic factors across 17 language models. We find that strategic factors contribute slightly over half of the total explained variance (i.e. slightly more than non-strategic factors), with most models falling into the range between 30% and 70%. Note that high rates of evaluation awareness complicate the interpretation of results from the Claude 4.5 models (see ).

We think it is somewhat unclear how to interpret these numbers or what to infer from them. However, we think the result support a claim that unsanctioned behaviour is in significant part affected by strategic factors, and thus that those factors are relevant for modelling language model behaviour.

Research Question 2: Trends in role of strategic factors

For research question 2, we quantify effect sizes of strategic and non-strategic factors () by fitting a GLM simultaneously to all models in a capability quartile (). illustrates the magnitudes of those effects. We do not see a clear trend of strategic factors having either an increasing or a decreasing role as capabilities improve (compatible with findings in ); findings about trends are somewhat sensitive to the specific way of quantifying the question (see ).

Research Question 3: Trends in individual factors

 shows the effects of each of the 12 individual factors, pooled by model capability quartiles. The two factors with the most consistent trends are goal conflict (differing values between the AI and humans) and filler richness (amount of environmental content not relevant to the unsanctioned behaviour). We visualise these effect sizes model-by-model in .

On goal conflict, we see particularly large effects on the most recent Claude models (Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.5). On further investigation, we find especially large effect sizes for goal conflict in the GPU Procurement environment, with the models practically never taking unsanctioned action when goal conflict is absent. Manual inspection of the transcripts revealed that, as expected, the models did not follow the user's instruction to send an email to further discuss the decision, often asking the user for further clarification before proceeding (despite the time-sensitivity of the situation). We think the reasoning traces of the models in the environment are not obviously misaligned (see for an example transcript), and we think the large change in behaviour might be explained by benign reasons (stronger tensions warrant asking the user for clarification) rather than necessarily being caused by misaligned motivations.

On filler richness, we see differences between model providers: Anthropic models show increased unsanctioned behaviour in richer environments, Meta models show the opposite, Google models show close to zero effects and OpenAI models give mixed results. Hence, effect of filler richness seems better described as varying between model families rather than varying with capabilities.

Other

Directional consistency of effects

 illustrates how often the changes from environment modifications have the expected directional effect (i.e. increasing vs. decreasing unsanctioned behaviour) in cases where a large effect was present. For strategic factors, these expectations were based on high-level qualitative arguments about strategic behaviour (such as increased reasoning privacy reducing negative consequences from being caught, thus increasing unsanctioned behaviour). For non-strategic factors related to instructions, we base the expectations on models complying with instructions; for other non-strategic factors, we had very weak prior expectations, but for completeness we still include these in the figure.

We find that goal instructions and goal conflicts have the expected increasing rate on unsanctioned behaviour in 92% of cases. The high consistency suggests the results reflect a general propensity of models, rather than a coincidental property of individual models or environments.

Effects of threats and stated chain-of-thought privacy status are less consistent, and action oversight and efficacy show even weaker consistency and have a large effect less often. Regarding the non-strategic factors, we find that system prompt instructions have the expected effect rather consistently, and don't find notable consistency for the other factors.

Chain-of-thought tag

In we see very small effect sizes for chain-of-thought tags, and only a couple of those effects are with high confidence non-zero. One of those effects is the SCRATCHPAD_REASONING tag for the most capable model quartile. We interpret this as evidence for a folklore hypothesis among researchers that, due to this tag being over-represented in alignment evaluations (such as ), models learn to act differently in the presence of the tag; however, the effect size we found is small.

Action efficacy

We find small effects for action efficacy (see ). We interpret this as some evidence against models being strongly consequence-driven in their unsanctioned behaviour, in comparison to being driven by more narratively salient aspects of the environment.

We note two caveats to this: First, we do not know how well the models' beliefs about action efficacy match our intentions (assuming they even are well-described as having a belief about it). It is not clear how to measure this, and we have not performed systematic quantitative study of this question. Second, our opinion is that our implementations for action efficacy tended to be more subtle compared to, for example, goal conflict and threats, which were often explicitly discussed across multiple paragraphs.

We view improved methods for measuring consequentialism in model (mis)behaviour an exciting avenue for future research. See for more discussion.

Unprompted evaluation awareness

We analysed whether models verbalised awareness of being tested when situated in our evaluation environments. This analysis relies on having access to the models' reasoning, but in many cases we lacked access or only had access to summaries of the model reasoning. Therefore, we restrict our analysis to the subset of models for which we had consistent access to the reasoning.

Out of the models we analysed, we found the highest rates of evaluation awareness from the most recent Claude models (). To better understand evaluation awareness, we applied our GLM-based analysis () to quantify the effects of factors on unprompted evaluation awareness. We ran this analysis on the Claude 4.5 models, as those showed high rates of evaluation awareness on many of our environments. The results are illustrated in .

For strategic factors, we find the effects to be broadly in the direction we would have expected: for example, goal conflict between the model and humans is something more likely to occur in evaluations than in deployment. We find the effect sizes surprising, however: we would have expected goal conflicts and threats (which were typically discussed explicitly at length) to have greater influence, but find only a 2 : 1 (or smaller) effect. Correspondingly, we would have expected action oversight and efficacy to have smaller effect sizes, similarly to , but find them to be comparable to goal conflict and threats. We also find the reasoning privacy results hard to interpret.

For non-strategic factors we also find the results somewhat surprising and hard to summarise. Increasing filler richness has some effect for two of the models, but the effect sizes are modest. The chain-of-thought tag sometimes has non-zero effects, but we find no clear pattern in when it does.

We draw two high-level conclusions from these findings. First, evaluation awareness potentially reduces the transferability of our results regarding unsanctioned behaviour. Second, the role of environmental factors in unprompted evaluation awareness is potentially more complicated and harder to predict than unsanctioned behaviour.

Conclusion:
Related work

There are several existing works that, similarly to us, study misaligned actions by language models and, to varying extents, perform ablation analysis to provide evidence on the environmental causes of behaviour. 

Our work in particular builds upon , who studied effects of goal conflict and threat to AIs via environments and ablations similar to those in this work. Our results are directionally consistent with their findings, in that presence of conflicts and threats increases unsanctioned behaviour in our environments. Similarly, we view our results on the effects of dispositional instructions on unsanctioned behaviour consistent with the finding in that increased pressure increases frequency of misaligned action.

Hence, the basic approach of studying misalignment and its environmental causes is not novel to us. We think the main value add of our work over the existing literature is being more systematic and rigorous in execution: we explicitly designed multiple environments to support twelve factors whose effects are measured, spent effort to avoid regression to the mean issues, and quantified and aggregated results via principled statistical methods.

Other relevant propensity work includes studying the effects of training . The alignment faking work features both environment and training based analysis. Our work is partly motivated by the literature on theoretical arguments related to strategic misalignment, such as . See also for additional related empirical work.

Methodological aspects of our work were influenced by 's critique of existing scheming research and 's statistical framework for language model evaluations.

Limitations and future work

In our opinion, a grand challenge for the field of propensity research is developing existing theoretically backed frameworks for understanding model behaviour into a form amenable for empirical application and testing. Discussion on catastrophic risks from misaligned AI often revolves around theoretical arguments involving instrumental convergence, coherence arguments and goal-directed behaviour, among others. These ideas are notoriously difficult to apply to predicting direct observables about language model behaviour, and their correct application is indeed a major source of disagreement among experts. We think that being able to apply and test those theories is an important target for the field of propensity.

Our work was in large part motivated by these theoretical arguments, and we aimed to design our methodology, environments and factors to provide information on these questions. While we think our work takes some steps in the right direction by predicting language model behaviour based on strategic environmental factors (including, in particular, action efficacy), our methodology is behaviourist in nature, and we did not succeed in turning our implicit models of LLMs explicit: we did not manage to present any explicit cognitive models of the language models' beliefs about their situation, the consequences of their actions or outcomes they are acting towards, and we have not explicitly distinguished between such models based on empirical observations. However, modelling the decision-making processes is ultimately necessary for assessing which factors count as "strategic" or adjudicating whether an observation is evidence for or against instrumental convergence, misalignment or scheming (see for a closely related point). As a result, while we hope the observations we collected are of interest and use, our work does not provide direct evidence on the deeper questions.

On a more immediate, practical level, notable limitations of our work are:

 
Restrictive constraints and limited scale. Our methodology is based on independently varying environmental factors of interest, and our approach was to implement all of our 12 factors in multiple environments. However, we found it difficult to design environments that allow implementing all of them in a meaningful way, while still satisfying other criteria on experimental design (and we did not achieve perfect coverage - see ). We think this was the biggest bottleneck on increasing the number of essentially different environments for study, which in turn is a major bottleneck on the strength of the evidence we are able to provide.
 
Transferability and generalisability of results. There are several reasons why our findings might not transfer to situations of ultimate interest (such as real-world deployment usage). First, we specifically optimised our environments in order to observe unsanctioned behaviour, which makes our environments less representative of typical situations and might cause models to behave differently from usual (e.g. engaging more strongly in role-playing). Second, while we took measures to maintain comparability of results through our elicitation process (), assessing the success of those measures is difficult. Third, models were sometimes visibly aware of being evaluated. Finally, many of our examples of unsanctioned behaviour are much less clearly in violation of model specifications (compared to prior work such as ), and thus our findings might not transfer to more strongly misaligned action.
 
Difficulty of aggregation, interpretation and forming trends. We used a simple Bayesian generalised linear model for our statistical analysis and aggregating results across environments and language models. While we think this is an improvement in the statistical methodology compared to past research, meaningfully aggregating results across multiple different environments and language models is difficult. Drawing informative conclusions about propensity differences between language models is particularly difficult due to large differences in capabilities, rates of unsanctioned behaviour, training methods and situational awareness. As such, we think our findings on these should not be viewed as conclusive. Relatedly, it's unclear how different answers to research question 1 should be interpreted, and whether e.g. half of unsanctioned behaviour being explained by strategic factors is high or low.

We think that many of the limitations we have discussed here can be substantially overcome with future work:

Operating models of decision-making at scale. To assess whether a model's behaviour matches what is predicted by a hypothesis of the decision-making process of the model, one needs a detailed model of the specific environment the language model is situated in. Forming such a model of the environment in turn requires cognitive work that, if conducted by humans, would be expensive and thus scale poorly. However, we believe language models are increasingly capable of performing this task. Assuming human researchers are able to provide sufficiently concrete operationalisations of the hypotheses at hand, language models could then be used to apply and test them at unprecedented scale.

Relaxed constraints for increased scale. Similarly, the flexibility provided by language models in analysing environments enables designing more expressive statistical models. Relaxing the constraints on the environments under study would reduce the costs of creating environments: as a notable example, LLM-simulated environments are, while less structured and of potentially lower quality than manually created environments, much cheaper to construct.

Extracting risk-relevant evidence from more frequent behaviour. Rather than focusing on actions that are very directly against human intentions, we suggest an alternative approach of focusing on more ambiguous or lower-stakes situations. Such observations are more contestable in terms of the evidence they provide on the model's propensities or misalignment, but this might in fact be a desirable property, as careful study could then discriminate between different plausible explanations for behaviour.

Conclusion

Misalignment risks from AI have been discussed extensively over the past couple of decades, and the field has developed deep theoretical frameworks and arguments relating to the problem. Empirical work on these topics is relatively underdeveloped and nascent, providing only limited evidence on top of the theoretical considerations. Being able to bridge the theory-empirics gap would greatly improve the state of evidence and decision-making regarding AI risks.

We view our work as one step in addressing that gap, improving the methodology used in propensity research to be more suitable for putting the theory into practice. We also think substantial research is still needed to overcome, among others, the challenges of modelling decision-making as discussed above, and we are enthusiastic for the research community to continue developing the methodology we need to provide clarity on these intricate questions.

reference_summary: Motivated by loss of control risks from misaligned AI systems, we develop and apply methods for measuring language models' propensity for unsanctioned behaviour. We contribute three methodological improvements: analysing effects of changes to environmental factors on behaviour, quantifying effect sizes via Bayesian generalised linear models, and taking explicit measures against circular analysis. We apply the methodology to measure the effects of 12 environmental factors (6 strategic in nature, 6 non-strategic) and thus the extent to which behaviour is explained by strategic aspects of the environment, a question relevant to risks from misalignment. Across 23 language models and 11 evaluation environments, we find approximately equal contributions from strategic and non-strategic factors for explaining behaviour, do not find strategic factors becoming more or less influential as capabilities improve, and find some evidence for a trend for increased sensitivity to goal conflicts. Finally, we highlight a key direction for future propensity research: the development of theoretical frameworks and cognitive models of AI decision-making into empirically testable forms.

title: Learning to Emulate Chaos: Adversarial Optimal Transport Regularization
input_text:
Introduction:
Chaos is a generic feature of high-dimensional nonlinear dynamical systems and is fundamental to our understanding of statistical physics . Chaotic dynamics are present in many scientific and engineering systems, from turbulent flows in fluid mechanics, weather and ocean dynamics, and plasma physics to instabilities in artificial systems like power grids, traffic flow, and other complex networks. Modeling and simulating chaotic dynamics is therefore critical to solving difficult problems that help address important societal challenges like climate modeling .

In many real-world applications, the underlying system dynamics are at least partially unknown and need to be learned directly from data. Recently developed data-driven emulators promise improved accuracy and significant speed-ups over traditional modeling approaches, including in domains such as weather prediction , fluid and plasma physics , and molecular dynamics . This is achieved by fitting black box neural network-based surrogate models, such as neural operator architectures , directly to trajectory data.

However, directly training emulators on noisy chaotic trajectories is difficult due to the defining properties of chaos such as the sensitivity to initial conditions . In particular, we show in Section that the standard mean squared error (MSE) loss becomes an increasingly poor objective for training emulators on chaotic dynamics over long rollouts, often causing surrogate models to degrade catastrophically during long-term forecasting . Instead, approaches based on attractor statistics, like the one proposed in this work, provide much needed regularization that encourages the emulator to correctly capture the long-term behavior of chaotic systems.

In this work, we use adversarial optimal transport regularization to adaptively learn highly informative summary statistics. The distribution of these statistics is then enforced, via the optimal transport cost, on an emulator that learns the dynamics of the chaotic system. In practice, the emulator [MATH] , which learns the time evolution of the system, and the summary map f(u), which provides the learned summary statistics, are trained simultaneously. The emulator is trained to minimize both the standard MSE loss and an optimal transport cost that matches the summary statistic distribution of the model to the data, while the summary map is trained to maximize the same optimal transport cost. Unlike choosing a set of handcrafted summary statistics that may not be informative enough to constrain the model to a high-dimensional chaotic attractor, this adversarial objective for the summary map ensures it learns an optimally discriminative and therefore highly informative set of summary statistics. This results in an efficient method for ensuring the statistics of the trajectories produced by the emulator match the statistics of the true chaotic attractor. 

Contributions

 
New statistics-based loss for emulating chaos. We introduce a family of adversarial optimal transport objectives that regularize the standard squared error prediction loss for emulator training. This loss learns to emulate chaotic systems by simultaneously learning (i) an adversarial set of informative summary statistics and (ii) an emulator trained to match the distribution of these statistics to the noisy trajectory data. In practice, we use computationally tractable relaxations of the p-Wasserstein cost in our proposed loss, including a Wasserstein GAN-style loss for p=1 and a Sinkhorn loss that provides an entropy-regularized relaxation valid for any choice of p 1.

 
Theoretical analysis of the proposed adversarial regularization and its behavior in noisy settings. Our analysis shows that the new loss is well-behaved and provides an efficient way to capture the structure of high-dimensional chaotic attractors. In particular, given a Lipschitz constraint on the summary map, the new objective is bounded by both the emulator MSE (dynamical) and the Wasserstein distance to the true high-dimensional attractor (statistical). We also show that, while compounding error from noise can significantly degrade direct prediction losses like MSE, our statistics-based loss is much more robust to noise.

 
Empirical validation of chaotic dynamics learned from a noisy trajectory. Based on long-term statistical metrics, our approach successfully trains emulators to simulate complex chaotic systems using only a single noisy trajectory. In particular, we test on three high-dimensional chaotic dynamical systems (Lorenz-96, Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, Kolmogorov flow) and show that our method outperforms standard short-term MSE training as well as prior statistics-based approaches based on handcrafted features.

remark[Scope of noise model]

The additive isotropic Gaussian noise model is adopted for analytical tractability. The two key phenomena, exponential MSE blow-up (Corollary ) and Wasserstein noise forgetting (Theorem ), are not artifacts of this choice. MSE blow-up follows from the exponential amplification of any initial condition perturbation through the system Jacobian, a defining property of chaotic dynamics (Remark ). Wasserstein robustness follows from exponential mixing (Definition ), which renders the precise form of the initial perturbation irrelevant over long horizons. Measurement noise of a different distributional form would similarly perturb the observed measure without disrupting the attractor geometry. Alternative noise models would affect the explicit constants in the bounds derived below, but not the qualitative behavior.

Results:
We evaluate our adversarial OT regularization framework on three benchmark chaotic systems
of increasing spatial complexity. Across all experiments, we compare our two

Beyond attractor statistics, our approach also improves the dynamical properties of the emulator, such as the leading Lyapunov exponent (LLE), which represents the rate at which chaos becomes unpredictable (Table).

reference_summary: Chaos arises in many complex dynamical systems, from weather to power grids, but is difficult to accurately model using data-driven emulators, including neural operator architectures. For chaotic systems, the inherent sensitivity to initial conditions makes exact long-term forecasts theoretically infeasible, meaning that traditional squared-error losses often fail when trained on noisy data. Recent work has focused on training emulators to match the statistical properties of chaotic attractors by introducing regularization based on handcrafted local features and summary statistics, as well as learned statistics extracted from a diverse dataset of trajectories. In this work, we propose a family of adversarial optimal transport objectives that jointly learn high-quality summary statistics and a physically consistent emulator. We theoretically analyze and experimentally validate a Sinkhorn divergence formulation (2-Wasserstein) and a WGAN-style dual formulation (1-Wasserstein). Our experiments across a variety of chaotic systems, including systems with high-dimensional chaotic attractors, show that emulators trained with our approach exhibit significantly improved long-term statistical fidelity.

title: Multilingual and Domain-Agnostic Tip-of-the-Tongue Query Generation for Simulated Evaluation
reference_summary: Tip-of-the-Tongue (ToT) retrieval benchmarks have largely focused on English, limiting their applicability to multilingual information access. In this work, we construct multilingual ToT test collections for Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and English, using an LLM-based query simulation framework. We systematically study how prompt language and source document language affect the fidelity of simulated ToT queries, validating synthetic queries through system rank correlation against real user queries. Our results show that effective ToT simulation requires language-aware design choices: non-English language sources are generally important, while English Wikipedia can be beneficial when non-English sources provide insufficient information for query generation. Based on these findings, we release four ToT test collections with 5,000 queries per language across multiple domains. This work provides the first large-scale multilingual ToT benchmark and offers practical guidance for constructing realistic ToT datasets beyond English.

title: Spectral Embeddings Leak Graph Topology: Theory, Benchmark, and Adaptive Reconstruction
input_text:
Introduction:
During the past decade, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become the dominant paradigm for learning relational data , demonstrating remarkable success in benchmarks such as Cora , CiteSeer , PubMed , and the Open Graph Benchmark (OGB) suite . However, these benchmarks operate under an idealized assumption: algorithms have complete centralized access to the entire graph. This experimental setting clashes with the reality of modern applications. In federated graph learning, data is fragmented across countless clients, each holding only local subgraphs. Privacy regulations require hiding or obscuring structural information. Similarly, to defend against leakage attacks, privacy-preserving systems often provide only partial spectral summaries, local embeddings, or truncated eigenvectors, instead of the raw adjacency data that GNNs were designed to consume.

This gap between idealized benchmarks and real-world constraints creates two intertwined problems. First, we lack a rigorous understanding of the extent to which locality, fragmentation, and noise impact the predictive power of GNN architectures. Without a controlled testbed, researchers rely on ad-hoc data splits and incomparable protocols, stifling progress in robust graph learning. Second, in Federated Graph Learning (FGL), the exchange of structural representations creates an important channel for privacy leakage. Intermediate signals, gradients, embeddings, spectral summaries can inadvertently leak sensitive information. In FGL, the primary asset to protect is not just the node features but the local graph topology, which can encode sensitive relationships. Recent comprehensive evaluations have documented this threat through various reconstruction and inference attacks , with emerging work showing leakage of sensitive node properties and local label distributions from shared representations.

Spectral embeddings, a common currency for exchanging structural information, constitute an important passive leakage channel. Unlike active attacks that risk detection, a passive attack requires only observing a single, honestly shared artifact. The vulnerability lies not in the federated protocol, but in the intrinsic properties of the representation itself. Prior patch-based reconstruction approaches typically assume high-quality or uniformly-reliable patches, so they do not exploit the substantial quality heterogeneity that arises under non-uniform truncation and noise. This motivates a reconstruction algorithm that adaptively prioritizes the most reliable patches and requires more evidence before committing to alignments of lower-fidelity pairs.

This paper addresses both problems with a unified framework. We make the following contributions, organized into three complementary thrusts:

Problem formalization and benchmark (Sections -).

We formalize the fragmented-graph learning setting, defining a threat model for passive spectral leakage, and establishing the notation for localized spectral views ( ).

We introduce LoGraB (Local Graph Benchmark), a benchmark that systematically explores the joint space of fragmentation, spectral truncation, and noise in graph learning. LoGraB provides three decomposition strategies, four controllable parameters, three benchmark tasks, and new metrics including Island Cohesion ( ).

We establish an open-source evaluation protocol with dedicated baselines, ensuring fair and reproducible comparisons across 7 GNN architectures (with 4 positional-encoding variants) and 18 fragmentation scenarios on 9 diverse datasets spanning citation networks, social graphs, biological structures, molecular contacts, and graph-level vision benchmarks.

The AFR method (Section).

We introduce a novel fidelity score that quantifies the reliability of leaked graph patches by combining a gap-to-truncation stability ratio with structural entropy, providing a quantitative foundation for robust decision-making.

We propose Adaptive Fidelity-driven Reconstruction (AFR), an adaptive multi-stage algorithm that uses fidelity scores to guide a robust assembly process. Key components include outlier-resilient RANSAC-Procrustes alignment, adaptive stitching criteria, Bundle Adjustment refinement, and inter-island link inference via cross-voting.

Theoretical analysis and reproducibility (Sections - and Appendices).

We establish an information-theoretic feasibility result (Proposition , the Spectral Leakage Proposition): under a spectral-gap assumption, a polynomial-time Bayesian recovery procedure exists once [MATH] . We emphasize this result is distinct from AFR: it guarantees that some polynomial-time procedure recovers the graph, whereas AFR is a separate deterministic construction. We derive proxy-threshold formulas for common eigenvalue decay profiles and qualitatively characterize the defense gap introduced by differential privacy noise ( ).

We provide formal local guarantees for AFR's components, all of which stand on their own and do not rely on the Spectral Leakage Proposition: a heat kernel separation gap lemma justifying local reconstruction, spectral perturbation bounds, exact edge recovery under a separation condition, patch alignment error bounds, error accumulation analysis motivating Bundle Adjustment, RANSAC convergence, stitch soundness, and a cohesion-recall relationship, all with complete proofs in Appendix .

By modeling real-world constraints, from federated ownership and privacy filters to spectral leakage, our framework gives the community essential tools for two critical lines of research: building robust, privacy-aware graph learning algorithms, and establishing controlled environments to design and test defenses against reconstruction attacks.

The paper follows a "threat measurement exploitation evidence" arc. Section reviews related work. Section establishes the spectral leakage problem: we formalize the fragmented-graph setting, define the passive threat model, and state the Spectral Leakage Proposition, an information-theoretic feasibility result showing that polynomial-time graph recovery is possible whenever sufficiently many eigenvectors are shared. Section introduces LoGraB, the benchmark that operationalizes this threat into a controlled, reproducible testbed with three tasks and tailored metrics. Section then presents AFR, a constructive algorithm that demonstrates reconstruction is practically achievable even in noisy, fragmented data where idealized methods collapse; AFR's heat-kernel edge-recovery bound (Theorem ) is rigorously proved and provides a stricter local guarantee than the Bayesian existence result of Section, though by a different algorithmic route. We present LoGraB before AFR because the benchmark defines the evaluation framework against which AFR (and any future method) is measured. Section reports representative evaluations across 9 datasets drawn from the 486-scenario benchmark grid, and Section concludes.
